WV12-P01.5.note: The author's own statements look forward with concern about the boards being lost to rot or scrap, not backward with longing, and no sentence praises or faults the lettering itself; read literally, none of the author's lines is ironic.

Whenever a jar marked Bertram turns up on my mother's table, I grin all over again at that swarm hanging among the pillowcases.
WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator laughs at the swarm and still grins at the memory; the hives are kept still, so nothing is lost to be wistful about, and Mrs. Pellow's wink reads as playful under either a literal or teasing reading, supporting amusement either way.

WV12-P04.5.note: The writer, still uncertain whether the chimney will survive, lies awake listening for falling brick, which is fear of a future loss rather than sadness over one that has happened, disapproval, amusement or admiration.
